prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: EN · Plan comparison (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 6 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 17px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Feature" · longest unbreakable word 63px · one-line width 93px
  col 2: header "Free" · longest unbreakable word 88px · one-line width 88px
  col 3: header "Pro" · longest unbreakable word 73px · one-line width 73px
  col 4: header "Enterprise" · longest unbreakable word 83px · one-line width 255px
  col 5: header "Notes" · longest unbreakable word 81px · one-line width 465px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 643px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 642px.
Fixed: content, font, 17px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""},"F":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

log.raw: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"All words stay intact, but Notes is starved into 5–7 lines while Free and Pro carry excess width, making rows unnecessarily tall and uneven."},"B":{"grade":"good","why":"Clean and readable: headers and values stay intact, Notes wraps to 3–4 lines, and column proportions are sensible, though Notes is slightly tighter than in D."},"C":{"grade":"bad","why":"Pro is too narrow, breaking “Unlimited” into “Unlimite d,” and Free breaks “Community”; mid-word breaks make the table look broken."},"D":{"grade":"excellent","why":"Balanced and publication-ready: Feature and all headers fit comfortably, no words break, and Notes has enough width to stay compact in 3 lines."},"E":{"grade":"good","why":"Very close to D: no broken words and compact Notes, but the Enterprise header is squeezed with almost no side breathing room."},"F":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"Notes is generously wide, but Feature is squeezed so “SSO / SAML” wraps and the Feature header is tight; the extra Notes width does not reduce line count."}},"best":["D"],"confidence":"high","unsure":"Pixel widths are inferred from the screenshots; D and E are very close, and reasonable viewers might prefer E's wider Notes despite its tighter Enterprise header."}
